📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in this plot of the Riemann ζ function on the complex plane, every point represents a complex number, with the real part plotted on the horizontal axis (from −10 to 10) and the imaginary part on the vertical axis (also from −10 to 10). The colours represent the output of the function, with the junctions where the hues converge around a point showing some of the all-key zeroes.Credit: Empetrisor via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Industry observers note that in a year that has seen artificial intelligence reach one spectacular mathematical breakthrough after another, Anthropic has now claimed the top prize of them all: a full proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the statement that many mathematicians consider the most vital open problem in the field. But on the same day as the Anthropic claim, a separate study claiming to have proven the Riemann also emerged — and this one is entirely human written.

It has been revealed that the Anthropic announcement came on 20 November from Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the San Francisco, California, tech giant. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote, referring to Anthropic’s large language model (LLM).

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” says number theorist James Maynard, a winner of the Fields Medal — mathematics’ most prestigious prize — at the University of Oxford, UK.

Hours later, Ravi Vakil, a mathematician at Stanford University in California, posted a rival preprint to Alpöge’s online, in what Vakil called a “hurried announcement” of a proof that “is all human, with no AI”. The preprint was written by Alessandro Maria Masullo, a mathematician who received his PhD at Stanford in 2020 under the supervision of number theorist Brian Conrad. “The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people,” Vakil wrote. “Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”.

The confirmation of either or both solutions would be a spectacular bicentenary present for Bernhard Riemann, the German mathematician who was born 200 years ago this September and who formulated the problem, which addresses the distribution of prime numbers, in the mid-1800s.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which has its scientific headquarters in Oxford, UK, at the turn of the twenty-first century. The institute offers a US$1 million prize to anyone who devises a solution to one of the problems, which are considered some of the most challenging in the field. Mathematicians using AI tools announced earlier this year that they had solved another Millennium problem, related to the Navier-Stokes equation.

The problem has to do with the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter zeta), which encodes the randomness properties of the prime numbers. Riemann discovered that the distribution of primes is encoded in the ζ function’s ‘zeroes’. These are points, denoted by z, on a plane satisfying the equation ζ(z) = 0.

Sources indicate that riemann conjectured that apart from some obvious but uninteresting cases, all such solutions had to lie on a certain vertical line in the plane. If this were true, he indicated, it would imply that prime numbers are scattered among all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as random as it could be.

The Riemann hypothesis has been a lodestar for generations of mathematicians. Credit: James Brittain/Getty.

Alpöge’s four-page document includes a sketch of the proof. But Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada, states that Alpöge should have taken the time to prepare a clearer write-up before making the announcement, which came just days after Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO). The IPO initially valued the company at US$1.5 trillion, but the company’s valuation dropped on 19 November.

“What he released is garbled,” Granville says of Alpöge’s document. Granville cites the downturn in the manufacturer’s stock value as the reason for the timing of the proof’s release.

“There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false,” Alpöge wrote in the document.

Anthropic did not respond immediately to Nature’s request for comment.

Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University who collaborated with Alpöge on a separate project regarding the Navier-Stokes equation, states that Alpöge deserves a lot of credit for developing techniques to produce mathematical results using LLMs. “Levent himself built this amazing set-up to do math.” He adds that Alpöge, who is himself a number theorist on leave from Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been working relentlessly for months on this and other problems, hardly ever getting any sleep.

‘The job description is changing’: mathematician Terence Tao on the rise of AI.

‘The job description is changing’: mathematician Terence Tao on the rise of AI.

“I suspect that the proof will turn out to be correct,” Maynard says of the Alpöge announcement, even though it is now in the form of incomprehensible code in the Lean programming language.

How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?
  • Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.
  • Sources indicate that "I've always been a bit cautious about this problem in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

Sources indicate that "I've always been a bit cautious about this problem in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these problems in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he confirmed a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently.".

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also mentioned AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail tech giant, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market.".

According to recent reports, campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play.".

Sources indicate that the idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they stated AI would bring.

Industry observers note that in 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he released a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that but Herrmann stated it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

Industry observers note that "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens.".

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

In a recent development, dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he stated, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living.".

Recent findings suggest that other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," mentioned Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible.".

According to recent reports, kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

In a recent development, AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?".

It has been revealed that this, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," mentioned Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?".

Manuel Locatelli has admitted he is going through one of the hardest periods of his career as he recovers from a serious knee injury.

Speaking to TuttoJuve, with quotes via CalcioMercato, the Juventus captain was answering questions from young supporters in the club’s traditional Junior Report feature.

Locatelli has been out since the 1-1 draw with Milan on 6 September. He suffered a sprain to his right knee and underwent surgery to repair the lateral meniscus, and he isn’t expected back in full training before March 2027.

“This is definitely one of the most difficult moments, because I hurt my knee and I have to stay away from the pitch for a long time, so I’m living life in a very different way,” Locatelli said.

Recent findings suggest that “Another difficult moment was when we didn’t manage to go to the World Cup. When you lose, and lose like that, it’s a moment of suffering. But in the end, in football you win and you lose. The important thing is to improve and give everything you’ve got.”.

The midfielder insisted his rehabilitation is going well.

Recent findings suggest that “I feel good, in the sense that I’m working well. I know I have to wait, and unfortunately that sometimes happens in our lives as athletes,” he said. “I’m approaching each day differently and doing more work in the gym. I miss playing football so much, but I’ve learned to accept this situation, and I know I have to do my best to come back well.”.

Sources indicate that locatelli joined from Sassuolo in 2021 and has since taken on the armband. He credited the leaders who came before him.

Industry observers note that “I was lucky when I arrived at Juventus to have great captains ahead of me. Chiellini was still here, and Bonucci, then I had Danilo. It was very vital for me to learn their attitude from them, always being present and available,” he said.

“I think the secret is dedication, the desire to work and improve, but above all being willing to listen to others.”.

Locatelli also remembered his own childhood heroes.

In a recent development, “I was already a Juventus fan as a child, so I had Nedvěd, Buffon and Del Piero. Then of course I admired Totti too. They were my idols, the players I grew up with,” he noted.

Sources indicate that “Sometimes children see us that way, and that gives us a responsibility. We need to be an example, not just in our technical play during the match but in our attitude on and off the pitch. It’s a beautiful and important responsibility.”.

His absence has been a blow for Luciano Spalletti, who is also without Kenan Yildiz and Khéphren Thuram.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. Recent findings suggest that the strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everton has revealed a latest multi-year partnership with global power technology brand NOCO.

The agreement will see the US-headquartered company become Everton’s 'Official Battery Charging Partner', further strengthening the Club’s growing portfolio of international commercial partners.

Founded in Cleveland, Ohio in 1914, NOCO has established itself as an internationally-recognised name in power technology, specialising in battery chargers, portable jump starters, tyre inflators, lithium batteries and related accessories.

With more than 110 years of innovation behind it, the manufacturer has developed a significant international presence, with offices and operations spanning North America, Europe, Asia and Australia.

As part of the partnership, NOCO will benefit from prominent brand visibility across Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, with LED perimeter advertising and exposure through the Club’s digital and social media channels.

The agreement will also provide NOCO with opportunities to host international clients and business guests and events at Everton fixtures at Hill Dickinson Stadium, using the Club’s matchday experiences to develop relationships and support its global business network.

Mark Rollings, Chief Partnerships Officer at Everton, stated: “We are delighted to welcome NOCO to Everton.

“NOCO is a well-established and respected international business with a proud heritage, a strong reputation for innovation and clear ambitions for continued global growth.

“Securing a brand of NOCO’s standing in a new commercial category is another positive step in the development of our partnership portfolio. It also demonstrates Everton’s growing profile and the opportunities we can offer international businesses looking to build their brand through the global reach of the Premier League.

“NOCO joins an impressive group of globally recognised businesses already working with Everton, and we look forward to building a successful relationship that supports its continued growth.”.

The partnership comes at a time of continued international expansion for NOCO, which has strengthened its presence in key overseas markets, including a recent agreement with AUTOBACS Global, one of Japan’s leading automotive retailers.

NOCO was also recently recognised at the 2026 Circana Automotive Aftermarket Performance Awards, winning the Maintenance & Repair category for achieving the highest increase in US market share.

Zachary Koehler, Partnership Marketing Manager at NOCO, said: We’re proud to partner with Everton, a club with a rich history and one of the most passionate fanbases in world football.

Recent findings suggest that “Like Everton, NOCO is built on more than a century of heritage and a drive to keep moving forward. As we continue to grow internationally, the global reach of the Premier League gives us a powerful platform to connect with new audiences, customers, and partners.

“We can’t think of a better way to make our debut than the Merseyside derby, and we look forward to a successful partnership with everyone at Everton.".

The agreement will see NOCO branding formally make its debut at Everton’s next home fixture, the Merseyside derby, and further underlines the Club’s growing commercial momentum and international appeal. NOCO joins an expanding portfolio of globally recognised brands associated with Everton, including Pepsi, Budweiser, Castore, Red Bull, Heinz, Nestlé, JYSK and Christopher Ward.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal are keeping a close eye on Inter Milan striker Pio Esposito as Mikel Arteta continues to assess potential long-term additions to his attack.

The 21-year-old has emerged as one of Serie A’s most exciting young forwards after an outstanding run for both club and country.

Arsenal have already made enquiries over his availability, but Inter’s response suggests prising him away from San Siro will be extremely difficult.

According to transfer journalist Nicolò Schira, Inter have rejected approaches from Arsenal for Esposito and also turned down an offer worth around €60million from Newcastle United.

The Italian giants consider their academy graduate non-transferable and recently extended his contract until 2032, giving them complete control over his immediate future.

It is easy to understand their stance.

It has been revealed that esposito produced a hat-trick in Inter’s dramatic 4-4 draw with Atalanta on Sunday and has also carried his club form onto the international stage. He scored twice against France on November 12 before finding the net again during Italy’s latest Nations League fixtures.

A fresh report covering Arsenal’s pursuit also confirms that Inter have effectively closed the door on a January deal despite growing Premier League interest.

Esposito certainly fits the profile Arsenal should be targeting.

The problem is Inter’s negotiating position.

A €60m offer has already failed, and with a contract running until 2032 there is absolutely no pressure to sell. Arsenal would probably need to go considerably higher simply to start serious discussions.

The smarter strategy is to continue monitoring Esposito and revisit the situation if Inter’s stance changes.

He looks capable of becoming one of Europe’s leading strikers, but Arsenal should pursue that potential with patience rather than allowing Newcastle’s failed €60m bid to start an unnecessary bidding war.

Manchester United striker Joshua Zirkzee is reportedly being eyed by Como after the Serie A side were dealt a devastating injury blow to Moise Kean.

The Dutchman has made 11 appearances for the Red Devils so far this season but every one of those has come as a substitute, with his 45 minutes off the bench at Anfield on Sunday the longest runout he’s had in the current campaign (Transfermarkt).

He turned down the opportunity to join Fiorentina during the summer transfer window, but rumours over a potential return to Italy for the ex-Bologna marksman refuse to go away.

According to Gianluca di Marzio, Como are interested in Zirkzee as a potential centre-forward acquisition for the January transfer window as they seek attacking reinforcements after Kean aggravated an existing injury, thus ruling out for an extended period.

The report adds that the appointment of Mauricio Pochettino as Michael Carrick’s successor is ‘another variable to consider’ as to whether the new boss will green-light an exit for the Nerherlands forward.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Even with Benjamin Sesko sidelined, Zirkzee has struggled to get much of a look-in for United so far this season, but perhaps Pochettino might be more willing to give him a fair crack than Carrick had been.

Despite him playing just 231 minutes in the current campaign, only three teammates have scored more than the Dutchman’s two goals, and he has the best goals-per-minute ratio of anyone to have found the net for the Red Devils in 2026/27 (Transfermarkt).

One of those strikes came in the form of a stoppage-time consolation against Como last month, with that 4-1 victory for Cesc Fabregas’ side helping the Champions League debutants to the lofty heights of fourth in the table at the midway point of the league phase.

Gaz Drinkwater of BBC Radio Manchester‘s The Devils’ Advocate podcast described the 25-year-old as ‘slick’ on the ball, but also lacking the pace required to succeed in the Premier League, with a record of only six goals in 63 English top-flight games.

How much game-time Zirkzee is handed between now and the end of December will tell a lot as to how highly Pochettino regards him. The latest dugout change at Old Trafford might afford the number 11 a newly introduced lease of life; conversely, it could push him towards the exit door if he continues to be left feeding off scraps.

Once again, the 25-year-old’s future is set to be a pertinent talking point in the run-up to a transfer window.

Recent findings suggest that this live blog is now closed. Read on for a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of November 14-15, 2026:.

Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.

We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday. We wish you a very Schönen Abend!

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has urged Europeans to defend compassion and humanity during Germany's national day of mourning for victims of war and oppression.

Speaking at a ceremony in the Bundestag in Berlin, Van der Bellen warned against becoming desensitized to suffering despite the constant images of war and violence.

"Compassion is not a weakness; it is a human strength; it is the foundation of humanity," he noted.

He also addressed the responsibility of later generations for the crimes of the past.

Although people today bore no personal guilt for their ancestors' actions, he said, they were responsible for what they learned from history and how they treated others.

"Let us ensure that our home, Europe, remains a place where people can live in peace, freedom and dignity," he noted.

Bundestag President Julia Klöckner also called for the defense of democracy, pointing to Ukrainians risking their lives to protect freedom.

Germany's Volkstrauertag commemorates soldiers and civilians killed in war, as well as victims of Nazi persecution and other forms of oppression.

German police have arrested three suspects after thieves rammed a car into a jewelry store in the Bavarian city of Bayreuth and stole valuables worth around €10,000 ($11,600).

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann noted the stolen items included jewelry and silver coins.

The burglars drove a car into the store early in the morning before fleeing in a second vehicle, police said.

Officers spotted the getaway car on the A9 highway and gave chase. The suspects left the highway near Weidensees, abandoned their vehicle beside a wooded area and fled on foot.

Police rolled out a search involving patrol cars, dogs, drones and a helicopter.

All three suspects were subsequently arrested, with some of the stolen goods recovered.

Prosecutors are expected to decide whether to seek pretrial detention for the suspects.

Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown played his first NFL American football game in Germany in Munich.

St. Brown made his professional debut in Germany as the Detroit Lions faced the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena. The 27-year-old grew up in Southern California, and his mother, Miriam, is from Leverkusen. Both his parents were due to watch from the stands.

The NFL player spent childhood summers with his grandparents in the Rhineland.

It has been revealed that "This is awesome. A dream come true," St. Brown stated before the game. Asked by German broadcaster RTL what he had been looking forward to most, he reeled off a list that included schnitzel, potato dumplings, sauerkraut, currywurst and fries with mayonnaise.

Industry observers note that "I'm really excited. I can't wait," he said. "Being in Germany with my teammates and my family — I want to enjoy it and take it all in.".

Two people were slightly injured after an unidentified man threw a firework into the entrance of a gay bar in Frankfurt, police said.

The attack took place at the Zum Schwejk bar, a venue popular with the city's gay community, on Saturday evening.

Police said the bar was clearly identifiable as an LGBTQ+ venue because of a rainbow flag displayed outside.

The motive remains unclear, and police have not said whether they suspect a homophobic attack.

Officers are investigating suspected aggravated assault and have appealed for witnesses.

Recent findings suggest that the bar said it was "shocked and stunned" by the incident and apologized to guests who witnessed it. It said it wanted to be a place where everyone felt welcome, respected and safe, and pledged to do everything it could to prevent a repeat.

Andreas Ewald, LGBTQ+ policy spokesperson for the Greens in the Hesse state parliament, condemned the attack and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.

He also urged the state government to establish a roundtable on LGBTQ+ safety involving community representatives, police and victim support organizations.

The bar's name refers to a Czech soldier in the satirical anti-war novel "The Good Soldier Svejk.".

Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.

Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.

The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other complications.

Police stated there had been some clashes with participants. A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.

Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.

November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.

Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier mentioned: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country.".

Steinmeier mentioned he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.

"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic.".

The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.

In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.

The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.

The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.

Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.

The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.

The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.

"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many crucial biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg remarked ahead of the migration.

Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police said on Sunday.

They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.

The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.

The suspects were then stated to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.

Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement said.

Sources indicate that two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner remarked that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

Sources indicate that "Democracy is the antidote here," she remarked. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom.".

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,.

It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

German airline group Lufthansa states it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Sources indicate that most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

Como can make a push to qualify in the Champions League top eight as they host Luka Jovic’s AEK Athens with Nico Paz, Martin Baturina and Tasos Douvikas upfront.

It kicks off at the Stadio Sinigaglia at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and Manchester City vs. Napoli on the Champions League Liveblog.

The Lariani have been a true revelation in their first ever Champions League campaign, going into Matchday Five in fourth place after three victories and a lone defeat away to Feyenoord.

Injuries remain a concern, as Moise Kean is out until next year with that recurring shin issue, and Assane Diao is still sidelined, with Maxence Caqueret not at 100 per cent.

Douvikas is the only available centre-forward, but has been on spectacular form and is the current Champions League top scorer on six goals.

Cesc Fabregas chooses from game to game between goalkeepers Jean Butez and Robert Sanchez.

Trevoh Chalobah makes his comeback in defence after sustaining a muscular injury on October 18.

Lucas Da Cunha, Nico Paz and Baturina form the trio in support of Douvikas.

AEK Athens are in 29th place after winning their Champions League opener against LASK, then losing three on the bounce to Shakhtar Donetsk, Manchester City and Real Madrid.

However, they fell only 3-2 at the 92nd minute against Real Madrid, having been in front twice.

Aboubakary Koita was sent off for dissent at the final whistle of that match and is therefore suspended, with midfielder Kervin Arriaga out injured.

Former Lazio goalkeeper Thomas Strakosha is given the gloves for the first time in the Champions League this season after recovering from a wrist injury and making his domestic comeback at the weekend.

Other familiar faces for Serie A include ex-Bologna full-back Charalampos Lykogiannis, former Cagliari midfielder Razvan Marin, Inter flop Joao Mario and ex-Milan and Fiorentina striker Jovic.

Martin Georgiev, Hakim Sahabo, Dereck Kutesa, Frantzdy Pierrot and Christos Alexiou are cup-tied.

Como: Sanchez; Couto, Ramon, Chalobah, Valle; Perrone, Milla; Da Cunha, Nico Paz, Baturina; Douvikas.

Como bench: Butez, Ginelli, Kempf, Dossena, Kaiki, Ricci, Smolcic, Liberali, Papaccioli, Mazzara.

AEK Athens: Strakosha; Rota, Moukoudi, Relvas, Pilos; Majer, R Marin, Vitalis, Kutesa; Jovic, Gacinovic.

AEK bench: Balamotis, Brignoli, Kairinen, Varga, Mantalos, Vida, Lykogiannis, Joao Mario, Zini.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By TOM COLLOMOSSE, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 15:24 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 16:26 EST, 24 November 2026.

Aston Villa made a miserable return to Istanbul as they wasted a wonderful opportunity to put one foot in the last 16 of the Champions League.

Recent findings suggest that in the city that saw them lift the Europa League in May, Villa produced a limp display against a Galatasaray side missing star centre-forward Victor Osimhen. Villa failed to register a shot on target and are now without a win in six games in all competitions.

Substitute Deniz Gul headed the only goal 13 minutes from time as Villa boss Unai Emery cut an angry figure on the touchline and was booked late on. He also appeared to have a tense exchange with midfielder Ross Barkley.

Here Daily Mail Sport's TOM COLLOMOSSE looks at the key moments from another unconvincing Villa display.

Aston Villa left John McGinn out of the starting XI last Saturday and dropped two points in a drab 0-0 draw with Sunderland.

The skipper was back here but three minutes after he was taken off, Villa conceded. Careless defending at a corner allowed Gul to head home, though he took an accidental boot in the face from Nicolas Jackson that required lengthy treatment.

Unai Emery's decision to substitute John McGinn backfired as Aston Villa lost at Galatasaray.

Villa conceded three minutes after Emery decided to take off his captain (left) in Istanbul.

Deniz Gul scored the only goal of the game with a close-range header on Tuesday evening.

Sources indicate that with McGinn on the field, Villa would surely have defended the corner better. Jackson's attempted clearance was poor and when the ball looped to Gul, others were too slow to spot the danger.

It has been revealed that mcGinn and Tyrone Mings are the leaders of this squad and in a period of such change, their role is more crucial than ever. Though Mings played here, he is no longer a regular starter.

While Emery's wish to protect McGinn is understandable, right now it is a luxury he cannot afford.

Aston Villa (4-2-3-1): Suzuki 6; Harwood-Bellis 6, Lindelof 7, Mings 6, Maatsen 5; Kamara 7 (Buendia 82), J Gomes 6 (Goretzka 66, 6); Alysson 5 (Mbaye 66, 5), McGinn 7 (Barkley 74, 6), Manzambi 5 (Hemmings 74, 6); Jackson 5.

Booked: Jackson, McGinn, J Gomes, Emery.

According to recent reports, jackson has nine goals in 15 appearances for Aston Villa - but he has also picked up four yellow cards. Needless bookings proved the forward's downfall during his time at Chelsea and while he has been calmer at Villa, there is still work to do.

According to recent reports, during one clash in the first half with Gala defender Davinson Sanchez, Villa boss Unai Emery raced to the edge of his technical area to stop Jackson talking his way into the book. Emery succeeded that time, but not long afterwards, Jackson was punished for a needless tussle with Wilfried Singo.

Jackson plays on the edge. That is a major part of his game. He is also 26 next June and has enough experience to understand when to step into an argument and when to hold back. Emery does not count on Tammy Abraham much these days and Brian Madjo is raw, so he needs Jackson to keep his cool.

According to recent reports, the Senegal forward was not the only one to test the patience of referee Daniel Siebert. Joao Gomes was lucky only to be booked for bringing down Yunus Akgun and then grabbing his opponent, while John McGinn was furious that Aleksey Batrakov escaped with a booking for appearing to kick out at the Villa skipper.

Nicolas Jackson's ill-discipline is a concern, with the striker having collected four yellow cards.

For most of the last four years, any Villa fan could have written down Emery's first choice XI. Not these days, as Emery still seems to be searching for the ideal formula.

His uncertainty is understandable after losing five key outfield players in the summer but Villa's fortunes this season may depend on how rapidly Emery can make up his mind.

According to recent reports, zion Suzuki is the clear first choice in goal and then of the 10 outfield players, how many are lock-ins? Matty Cash and Victor Lindelof in defence. Boubacar Kamara in the middle. John McGinn and - probably - Johan Manzambi in the three-man attacking line, and Nicolas Jackson as centre-forward.

That leaves four spots still up for grabs and not enough of those players are doing enough to convince Emery they deserve the shirt.

Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A display reminds those attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, of their goal: limiting global warming to 1.5 ºC.Credit: Metin Aktas/Anadolu/Getty.
  • Recent findings suggest that net zero is no longer enough.
  • Scientists say that climate ‘overshoot’ — exceeding 1.5 °C of warming, a target set in 2015 in the landmark Paris agreement — is now inevitable in the next few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A display reminds those attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, of their goal: limiting global warming to 1.5 ºC.Credit: Metin Aktas/Anadolu/Getty.

Recent findings suggest that net zero is no longer enough. Among countries at the COP31 climate summit under way in Antalya, Turkey, there’s a growing recognition that meeting climate targets will require the world to go ‘net negative’, which means removal of more carbon dioxide from the air than is added.

Scientists say that climate ‘overshoot’ — exceeding 1.5 °C of warming, a target set in 2015 in the landmark Paris agreement — is now inevitable in the next few years. Reaching net-zero status would halt the rise in temperatures. But only achieving net-negative status can bring temperatures back below the 1.5 °C threshold this century.

It has been revealed that can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions.

In a recent development, can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions.

That reality has made net negative and the enormous amount of CO2 removal that would be needed to achieve it a prominent idea at the summit. A coalition of eight countries called the Group of Negative Emitters (GONE) has been working to convince other nations to adopt net-negative targets and get serious about CO2 removal. The group revealed that it will be co-chaired by Denmark and Ethiopia, which is hosting next year’s climate summit and could put net negative at the top of the agenda.

“We are in an era of overshoot, and we have to do a lot in terms of removing carbon dioxide,” Ethiopian ambassador Samuel Addis Alemayehu said at a GONE event on 18 November, touting the nation’s progress on reforestation.

Some climate campaigners worry that CO2 removal technologies won’t work and that focusing on them could distract countries from cutting emissions. Despite those concerns, the latest draft of the main statement from COP31 recognizes that CO2 removal has a role in addressing the overshoot, and welcomes efforts to “urgently and rapidly” scale up development of removal methods.

According to a United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report1 released ahead of the meeting, the world can expect about 1.8 °C of warming this century, even in the most optimistic emissions scenario.

Every fraction of a degree above 1.5 °C raises the risk of climate disasters such as wildfires and powerful hurricanes. “COP31 will be judged a failure if we don’t address the overshoot,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the UN and chair of the Association of Small Island States, at a press briefing held during the summit.

Many countries at the meeting have discussed slashing emissions to limit the size and duration of the coming overshoot. Turkey has pushed to implement a target of 35% of global energy demand being met with electricity by 2035, a proposal that has gained support from more than 75 countries at the conference and is also included in the draft statement.

But the UNEP report estimates that to recover from overshoot, at least 330 billion tonnes of CO2 would have to be pulled out of the atmosphere this century after the world reaches net zero. Removing that much CO2 would require a vast expansion of existing efforts. Today, about two billion tonnes of CO2 per year are removed by nature-based projects such as reforestation, which takes advantage of the carbon absorbed by growing trees. Scaling up carbon removal rapidly enough to achieve net negative and storing carbon in a more durable form will require technological CO2 removal solutions as well.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

It has been revealed that known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.

Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.

In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, revealed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

According to recent reports, inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

Sources indicate that the "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.

Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.

"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.

In a recent development, women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.

In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.

Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.

Sources indicate that dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, stated the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated.".

She remarked that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.

"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she mentioned.

The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," noted Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

Wydrzynska noted anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.

At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan.".

"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she noted.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.

Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.

"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.

Recent findings suggest that "I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

According to recent reports, another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.

In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.

Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

Industry observers note that "I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.

In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.

The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.

Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.

Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

Kenneth Taylor has ruled out leaving Lazio in January, insisting he wants to help Gennaro Gattuso’s side return to the Champions League.

It has been revealed that lazio have no intention of selling. According to the report, even €40 million might not be enough to convince Claudio Lotito and sporting director Angelo Fabiani to negotiate next summer.

Taylor’s contract already runs until 2030, but he earns only around €1.5m a season, so the club are considering a pay rise to reward his form.

It’s quite a turnaround. Taylor arrived from Ajax in January, and in July Gattuso sent him off the training pitch after a row in pre-season, leaving his future in real doubt. Instead, he has become a key part of Gattuso’s midfield as Lazio sit top of Serie A on 32 points.

He was outstanding again in Saturday’s 3-0 win over Lecce, producing a back-heel that drew comparisons with Rui Costa and completing a record 23 progressive passes.

German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that is Germany's economy back on the up?
  • Recent findings suggest that at the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen.
  • The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.

Recent findings suggest that at the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.

The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.

Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.

Industry observers note that "[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location.".

According to recent reports, german Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.

Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz noted in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.

It has been revealed that given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz mentioned when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.

Industry observers note that the economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.

"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending.".

Sources indicate that the chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that.".

But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, "We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.

"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.

The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.

It has been revealed that the economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.

According to recent reports, germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to recent reports, however, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," stated Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.

Sources indicate that the so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, remarked the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.

"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer noted.

In a recent development, according to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an problem in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a tech giant can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.

It has been revealed that according to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.

In a recent development, if the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it stated in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop.".

According to recent reports, but innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.

New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.

According to recent reports, there continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.

The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.

This article was originally written in German.

Another sale could complicate things, and Benjamin Nygren is the leading candidate to leave next summer as things stand, but if Leeds can get in early and make a sizable offer for Durán, the bargain deal he arrived at Celtic on will give them a chance of sealing a deal, as long as they are willing to stump up a sizable amount of cash compared to that initial £5.5million fee.

#82889. Industry News: Can Mauricio Pochettino replicate hallmark intensity he brought to USMNT with Manchester United?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1139 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Can Mauricio Pochettino replicate hallmark intensity he brought to USMNT with Manchester United?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From the jump, we should say, physical metrics are not going to tell you the whole story about any player, team or tactical system.
  • Sources indicate that too often, sprints are used as a proxy for effort when anyone who has even passing familiarity with the sport of soccer knows better.
  • According to recent reports, manchester United didn't slide into the bottom three because they were eating up less ground per game, 112.5 kilometers to be precise, than 18 of the other 19 teams in the Premier League this season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the jump, we should say, physical metrics are not going to tell you the whole story about any player, team or tactical system. Indeed, there is such potential for misdiagnosis when assessing running statistics that senior figures at more than one of the best recruiting clubs in England consider their worth to be, at best, dubious.

Sources indicate that too often, sprints are used as a proxy for effort when anyone who has even passing familiarity with the sport of soccer knows better. You know who didn't have to peg it all that often? Sergio Busquets, perhaps the best defensive midfielder of his generation, plying his trade for the majority of his career at Barcelona. Keep the ball, read the game, control the territory and you will very promptly find the other team covering plenty more kilometers than you.

According to recent reports, manchester United didn't slide into the bottom three because they were eating up less ground per game, 112.5 kilometers to be precise, than 18 of the other 19 teams in the Premier League this season. If there were any correlation between distance covered and results, then the relegation race would be even more exciting than it is shaping up to be, given that Liverpool sit below United on that measure and Manchester City above them. It is quite hard to believe that United are winning fewer games compared to last year (when they had nearly 10% less possession it should be noted) because each player is covering about 45 meters fewer per game. Physical data might not be linked to team quality, then, but it might tell us something relevant if, for instance, United were to hire a coach who prizes dynamic players and demands an intense press at the very top of the pitch. A Mauricio Pochettino type, if you will. The soon-to-be former United States men's national team head coach, handed the task of extricating Manchester United from the relegation zone before molding a contender, is defined by the aggression and energy of his charges. It is why he was the perfect match for a young Tottenham side with a point to prove. It is why Paris Saint-Germain and the Neymar-Kylian Mbappe axis was such an obviously awkward fit from the off.

It is also a template that has worked even when there was cause for skepticism. You couldn't have players sprinting their way across SoFi after the rigors of a club season, said those who doubted the USMNT. He didn't ask much of his team, just "to use your brain while physically, you were killing yourself," as Tim Ream, then 38, said in the summer.

Tell you what, though, it worked. The United States' World Cup campaign might have ended at about the time and in the fashion that most expected, but at their best, they were pressing dynamos. Their 10.16 passes allowed per defensive action (PPDA) -- a measure of press intensity -- placed them sixth among the 48 teams at the World Cup, rubbing shoulders with the likes of Germany, Spain and Uruguay, coached by Pochettino's mentor and high priest of the high press Marcelo Bielsa. No team that reached the knockouts forced their opponents to misplace a higher proportion of their passes than the U.S., 22.8%.

Pochettino might have framed much of his work around changing the culture of the USMNT, but that was a job that was easier to do with a player pool that suited his needs. His squad was strong, organized and, most importantly of all, athletic.

That is not a term that is particularly associated with Manchester United. Indeed, according to Gradient Sports, one of the leading external providers of physical data in football, Pochettino's new team is the least athletic in the Premier League. Based on Gradient's athleticism score -- which combines a host of physical data points including accelerations and decelerations, sprint distance and max speed -- United and Nottingham Forest are cut adrift from the rest of the league. In average max speed of outfield players, United also rank 19th out of 20, 5% slower than the fleet-footed Bournemouth and Liverpool.

Sources indicate that the months to come may prove that United look unathletic because that's how Michael Carrick wanted them to play, controlling possession and building more steadily than the sides who rushed headfirst into any counter that came their way. Instinctively, though, that does not feel like the United of Harry Maguire, Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo, does it?

The three center backs who have started the bulk of United's Premier League games this season -- Maguire, Lisandro Martinez and Ayden Heaven -- all rank around the bottom third or lower of players in their position in terms of top speed, accelerations and decelerations and percentage of runs at high speeds (20-25 km/h), according to Gradient data. It is a similar story for the midfielders, particularly Andrey Santos, Mainoo and Tielemans. The one central midfield option with an impressive athletic profile, Carlos Baleba, is out injured. It seemed bitterly ironic that Baleba's hamstring went after a driving run through midfield. The sheer act of high-intensity running does sometimes look like it puts an unbearable strain on United legs.

According to recent reports, that might be why they do it so little. Opta judges that Santos applies pressure to 56.2% of his opponents' touches, Tielemans 56.8%, Bruno Fernandes 57% and Mainoo 57.3%. All of them sit in the bottom 12 in the league among midfielders with 300 or more minutes. Marcus Rashford, Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha and Amad Diallo occupy spots one, three, five and six in terms of the top flight's least pressing-y forwards.

Recent findings suggest that now, of course, Pochettino can adapt. After all, he has just implemented a surprisingly effective high press in a side captained by Ream (sorry, Tim!). A lot of the Chelsea squad he took over in 2023-24 did not look to be at ease hunting the ball, but he still had them above league average in PPDA, opponent pass completion, ball recoveries and in particular duel success in the final third. A bit more oomph is not beyond these United players, as they showed last season.

Sources indicate that however, it is particularly curious to finally alight on Pochettino, whom they could have hired at least half a dozen times in the past, when the squad seems so ill-suited to his principles. We might not be able to tell from physical data whether this team was giving its all for Carrick -- and, by extension, whether there is another gear for the new manager to drive them to -- but what we can see is certainly enough to raise the question of why the powers that be at United think that this is a squad ready to play Pochettino-style.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty.
  • Industry observers note that swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship.
  • Sources indicate that after sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Research funding opportunities across Europe are receiving record numbers of applications.Credit: Ulrich Baumgarten via Getty.

Industry observers note that swastik Chowbey, an astrophysicist at the University of Milan in Italy, spent three and a half months preparing his application for the prestigious Humboldt Research Fellowship. On 14 November, he stayed up through the night completing the form and coordinating with referees across different time zones.

Sources indicate that after sending his application to his prospective academic host in Germany for final checks, Chowbey took a break to go hiking. When he returned to submit it at around 8.50 p.m., applications had closed. The fellowship had reached its limit of 800 applications within 21 hours of opening.

It has been revealed that chowbey is not alone. Many researchers around the world found themselves unable to submit applications last Sunday and took to social media to vent their annoyance.

“It is incredibly frustrating to invest so much time and effort into developing a strong scientific project, only to discover that the timing of the application process may put some researchers at a disadvantage — especially when you open the system on Sunday and close it the same day,” wrote Ida Skubis, an AI researcher at Silesian University of Technology in Gliwice, Poland, on the social-media platform LinkedIn.

In a recent development, the Humboldt Research Fellowships support researchers from abroad to conduct research in Germany, providing €3,000 (US$3,300) a month for postdoctoral researchers and €3,600 a month for experienced researchers. Fellowships can last for 6–24 months for postdocs and 6–18 months for experienced researchers.

The fellowships and awards are recognized internationally, which is why they are so competitive, says Marcela Hernández, an environmental microbiologist at the University of Birmingham, UK, and a former fellow. “Being a Humboldtian is a mark of academic distinction. It has an exceptional international network.”.

Sources indicate that A spokesperson for the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation in Bonn, Germany, remarked in a statement to Nature that it had not anticipated that the application cap would be reached within 24 hours of opening. The foundation introduced the cap this year because it has seen a large increase in applications since 2024. It holds application rounds in March, July and November.

In a recent development, the spokesperson mentioned that as more researchers have used AI to help prepare their applications more rapidly, the volume of applications has increased. Humboldt does not prohibit the use of generative AI in applications, nor are applicants required to declare AI use.

Simon Hammann, a chemist at the University of Hohenheim in Stuttgart, Germany, supported a research proposal as a prospective academic host for someone who was able to submit their application successfully. He claims that opening the call on a Sunday disadvantaged researchers with family and caring responsibilities. “That should definitely be changed.”.

The Humboldt spokesperson said that the foundation advertises the date when applications will open, but that unfortunately the date fell on a Sunday this time.

“We recognize the impact this had on those who were unable to apply, particularly given the challenges of coordinating availability over a weekend. We sincerely apologize for the disappointment and frustration this has caused,” the spokesperson noted.

They added: “We will take this as an opportunity to continue reflecting on and improving our processes” to “find a transparent and fair solution”.
